newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bosnian Serb threats unacceptable - U.S. diplomat.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serb threats unacceptable - U.S. diplomat.

text.p: The U.S. ambassador to the United Nations said on Thursday that any Bosnian Serb attempts to retaliate against world leaders for stepping up their hunt for indicted war criminals would be intolerable.

Ambassador Bill Richardson said he had heard reports that violent threats had been made to leaders of states contributing to the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) including U.S., British and German forces in Bosnia.
He told journalists such threats were a well-known tactic of the Bosnian Serb leadership, which is loyal to former president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic, who is now in hiding.
"Those threats are unacceptable," Richardson said during a visit to Bonn.

"There are a number of reports involving violence. I can't comment specifically on individual threats. But it is well-known that the leadership in (Bosnian Serb) Pale has used these intimidation techniques within their own population."

International monitors and peacekeeping soldiers have been targeted by a series of small-scale explosions over the past two weeks since a NATO raid on two Serb suspects wanted by the United Nations for war crimes.

A German newspaper reported on Wednesday that Germany, Britain and the United States were concerned about the safety of top government officials. It named Chancellor Helmut Kohl and other German officials as being at risk.

The Die Welt daily said there was talk in German security circles of "increased threats" by Bosnian Serbs to mount violent attacks on Bonn, London and Washington now that they were taking a tougher approach to bringing war criminals to book.
British troops in the NATO-led peace Stabilisation Force (SFOR) in Bosnia shot dead a former police chief in the town of Prijedor this month after he fired on them to resist arrest.
They also arrested a hospital director there wanted for complicity in genocide against Bosnian Moslems and Croats during the 1992-95 war.

The incidents drew quick condemnation from the Bosnian Serb leadership but praise from the United Nations war crimes tribunal in the Hague, which had urged SFOR forces to harden their resolve to catch alleged criminals.
Richardson, who had just visited Bosnia, said SFOR was making progress in implementing the Dayton peace accord and on bringing indicted war criminals to justice.
"We are pressing all parties (to hand over their war criminals). We've got to make progress and I think the allies have shown we're serious about this in Prijedor," he said.
During the trip he arranged a meeting between Croatian President Franjo Tudjman and Moslem chairman of the Bosnian presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, on August 6 after several months of delay.
Richardson criticised Karadzic for having a powerful influence on the Serb part of Bosnia and said it was a serious obstacle to peace.

"Karadzic is playing a very negative role and is a constant obstruction. We see this in his political poster campaign, which violates Dayton, and in intimidation techniques and random acts of violence," Richardson said.
